The new beryllium plasma facing surface represented approximately 40 m^2 of the ~80 m^2 replaced by the ITER-like wall.
The target iron concentration for the beryllium material was 0.075%.
The optimum castellation size was 12 mm x 12 mm square and 16 mm deep with a half-round profile.
Disruptions produced changes in magnetic field of the order of 100 T/s, inducing significant eddy currents in the beryllium tiles.
The beryllium tiles have an electrical resistivity of ~0.08 μΩm at 200°C, much lower than the ~10 μΩm for the previous carbon tiles.
The design limit for the exposed depth of the beryllium tile edges was ~40 μm, combined with a minimum achievable cut width of 350 μm.
Vacuum-cast Inconel 625 was selected as the material for the tile carriers, as a compromise between cost and material properties.
227 anomalies were recorded during the ITER-like wall installation, with 159 resulting in non-conformance reports and modifications.

For the higher elongation limiter configuration, the monitored temperature stayed below 760°C, though some beams outside the monitored regions reached much higher temperatures with melting damage observed.
Disruptions were more threatening due to the reduced radiative losses compared to carbon, leaving most of the plasma magnetic energy to be conducted to the wall.
Slide-away electron beams due to lack of fuelling following an emergency coil shutdown caused the melting of 1-2 castellations on the inner wall guard limiter.
The design predicted a 20-30% contribution to the temperature increase due to edge heat flux, but experiments showed ~50% additional increase near the exposed edges.
Restarting the plasma on the ITER-like wall proved much easier than for the carbon wall, with no further conditioning required after the first plasma and no deconditioning by disruptions.
The JET facility had ~4000 kg of beryllium available for re-use, which helped achieve the target iron concentration of 0.075%.
Preproduction prototypes, jigs, and mock-ups were extensively used to validate the design and installation procedures for the beryllium PFCs.
